name: Conservatism
summary: Conservatism, in the sense its defining sources give the word, is a disposition and a tradition of thought that distrusts abstract political reasoning and revolution, trusting inherited institutions, custom, prescription and prudence, and accepting only gradual, discriminating change. It holds that an enduring moral order and a constant, imperfect human nature limit what politics can achieve, prizes private property, local community, religion and the checks that restrain power, and accepts natural and institutional differences against levelling.
scope: Burkean conservatism as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy defines the narrow sense: the line from Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France through Coleridge, Oakeshott and Scruton, together with Russell Kirk's own account of its principles. Following the SEP, which says American right-wing thought is largely neo-conservative and libertarian rather than Burkean, it leaves out neo-conservatism, libertarianism, reaction (de Maistre), fascism, and party platforms; where these defining sources are silent on a policy question, the answer is null.

notes: Rebuilt on rules 7 from three defining sources saved in scratchpad/sources/conservatism/: the SEP entry, Burke's Reflections (volume 4 of the Works) and Kirk's Ten Conservative Principles. The first pass's answers rested mostly on Wikipedia summaries and guesses about contemporary parties; each was kept only where these sources state a position and was otherwise nulled with its reason in the statement's review history. Goldwater's The Conscience of a Conservative was read but not cited, because the SEP treats American right-wing thought as largely neo-conservative and libertarian rather than Burkean, so it is outside the defining sources' scope. Themes searched: economy (property, levelling, confiscation, planning), government (monarchy, hereditary rank, Lords, representation, checks on power, revolution), society and religion (established church, atheism, family, equality), world, ecology (conservation) and technology (change). Burke and Kirk are silent on most economic policy, foreign affairs, criminal justice, gender, immigration and technology questions, so those are null and the uncertainty rule is expected to fail.
